extracted.intended_audience: People or organizations seeking to write public interest comments that improve regulators' knowledge of the economic consequences of proposed regulations (advocates, analysts, think tanks, interested citizens).
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing public-interest comments on proposed federal regulations that use economic analysis to support each claim and maximize influence on regulatory decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive, information-rich comments
rubrics_metrics.description: A constructive, information-rich comment that clearly communicates and supports its claims is more likely to have an impact on regulatory decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote from federal government tips emphasizing that comments should both communicate clearly and support claims with evidence. Use this as an overarching standard for tone and content: be constructive rather than purely adversarial, provide information, and back assertions with support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the regulatory process
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand how federal regulations originate and the procedures agencies must follow when writing regulations, including economic analysis requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know that regulations originate from laws passed by Congress and that agencies are delegated lawmaking authority. Consult the Unified Agenda of Federal Regulatory and Deregulatory Actions to see what rules are under development (but be aware items can remain listed for years or that some proposed rules were never listed). Recognize that agencies often must perform economic analysis of proposed rules and that helping agencies get the economic analysis right can influence regulatory decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciate the agency’s definition of the 'public interest'
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and take into account the regulatory agency’s own conception of the public interest when framing your comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor arguments and economic analysis to align with or directly address the agency’s statutory mission, priorities, and how it defines public interest in the context of the rulemaking; this increases relevance and persuasiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the key topics a good economic regulatory analysis should address
rubrics_metrics.description: Be familiar with the main topics and analytical elements that constitute a sound economic regulatory analysis so your comment can address them effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and respond to the specific analytical dimensions agencies are expected to consider (costs, benefits, alternatives, distributional effects, baseline assumptions, data sources, modeling choices). Even if the guide lists further specifics elsewhere, the core idea is to target the standard topics of regulatory economic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the agency’s legal authority and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the legal environment in which the agency operates, including the agency’s statutory authority and judicial or statutory constraints on its actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should reflect knowledge of what the agency is legally authorized (and not authorized) to do; identify legal boundaries and constraints that limit or shape feasible regulatory options, because these affect which economic arguments are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write the comment in the appropriate format, language, and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare your submission using the format, language, and tone that will be constructive and accessible to agency staff and likely to influence decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine clear writing with supported analysis. Use plain language, structure arguments logically, be concise where possible, and avoid unnecessary jargon. Ensure claims are supported by data or analysis and presented in a format (summary plus appendices/data/methods) that facilitates agency review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use substantive economic research presented in the right format
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide substantive economic research (analysis, data, models) and present it in a format that agencies can use and evaluate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-documented economic analysis — with transparent methods, sources, assumptions, and, where applicable, model code or data appendices — is more likely to be influential. Present results so agency analysts can assess and, if appropriate, replicate or incorporate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell other interested parties about your comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Inform and engage other stakeholders about your submitted comment to increase visibility and potential influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disseminate your comment to interested parties (advocacy groups, media, academic networks) so they can reference, support, or amplify your analysis; coordinated attention can increase the chance that agencies notice and consider the points raised.
